title: Conditional probability
example: For a fair die: P(even | greater than 3) = 2/3, since {4,5,6} contains two even outcomes.
note: The vertical bar means “given”, not division or absolute value. Assume P(B) > 0.
wrong: The probability that either A or B happens.
The probability of B given A.
The probability of A multiplied by the probability of B.

title: Joint probability
example: On a fair die, “even AND greater than 3” gives {4,6}, so the probability is 2/6.
note: Do not automatically multiply P(A)P(B); that requires independence.
wrong: The probability that at least one of A or B happens.
The probability of A given B.
The probability that neither event happens.

title: Distribution of a random variable
parts: The count X follows a Poisson distribution with parameter λ.
note: The tilde states a probability law.

title: Expected value
parts: The probability-weighted mean value of X.
example: A fair six-sided die has mean (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5.
note: An expectation can be a value that X cannot take.
wrong: The most likely single value of X.

title: Variance
parts: The expected squared deviation from the mean of X.
example: If X is 0 or 2 with equal probability, its mean is 1 and Var(X)=1.
note: Squaring deviations stops positive and negative values cancelling.
wrong: The mean of the unsquared deviations.

title: Cumulative distribution function
parts: The probability that X takes a value at most x.
example: On a fair die, the cumulative probability at 3 is 3/6=0.5.
note: For a discrete variable, the probability at x is included.
wrong: The probability X equals x exactly.

title: Binomial distribution
parts: X counts successes in n independent trials with the same success probability p.
example: For two fair coin tosses, X∼Bin(2,0.5) and P(X=2)=0.25.
note: X counts successes rather than recording the trial number of the first success.
wrong: X records which trial first succeeds.

title: Independent events
parts: The chance both independent events happen
equals the product of their probabilities.
example: Two independent fair tosses are both heads with chance ½×½=¼.
note: Independent events with positive probabilities cannot be mutually exclusive.

title: Markov transition probability
parts: The probability of going from i to j in one step of a time-homogeneous Markov chain.
example: If rain follows a sunny day 30% of the time, pₛᵣ=0.3 in a two-state model.
note: The current state is after the bar and the next state is before it.
wrong: The probability of going from j to i in one step.

title: Bayes’ rule
parts: The chance of A given B
is the reverse conditional times the prior divided by the chance of B.
note: Swapping the event and condition generally changes the probability.
wrong: P(A given B) always equals P(B given A).
